title: Countdown to History: India's First Private Orbital Rocket Set to Launch
summary:
In a milestone for India's commercial space sector, Skyroot Aerospace is poised to launch Vikram-1, the nation's first privately built orbital rocket. Liftoff is set for 2 a.m. EDT (11:30 a.m. IST) on July 18 from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre on Sriharikota Island. You can watch the historic event live via Skyroot's stream starting at 12:45 a.m. EDT.

Founded in 2018, Skyroot made headlines in 2022 with its suborbital Vikram-S rocket, becoming the first private Indian company to reach space. Vikram-1 is a significant leap: a four-stage, seven-story-tall small-satellite launcher capable of hauling about 770 pounds (350 kg) to low Earth orbit. "The small satellite launch market is deeply constrained on the supply side," said CEO Pawan Kumar Chandana. "At the same time, the demand for services enabled by satellites in space will only continue to grow."

The test flight, dubbed Aagaman (Sanskrit for "Arrival"), aims to validate the rocket's systems. But it's not flying empty. Payloads include a technology demonstration from German company DCUBED, the Solaras S3 nanosatellite pathfinder from Indian startup Grahaa Space, and Embrace—a robotic arm from Cosmoserve Space designed to capture space debris. Skyroot's own SCOPE satellite will collect flight data. Two symbolic payloads add flair: an 18-karat gold rocket sculpture and "Cosmic Bloom," a jewelry piece with lab-grown gems.

"What we are aiming to do on 18 July is bigger than a single launch," said COO Naga Bharath Daka. "It represents the hopes and hard work of around 1,000 people, the contributions of over 400 suppliers, and nearly 3,000 days of resolve." Both Daka and Chandana are former Indian Space Research Organisation engineers, bringing deep expertise to the venture.

The launch window extends to August 4, providing flexibility. If successful, Vikram-1 could position Skyroot as a reliable, on-demand launch provider for the global small-satellite market, blazing a new trail for India's space ambitions.
why_it_matters: The success of this launch could make space access cheaper and more available, enabling more satellites for climate monitoring, internet connectivity in remote areas, and even inspiring you to pursue a career in space tech – which might soon be as common as a software startup.

background_read: India's space program, led by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO), has a long history of successful missions, including sending a low-cost orbiter to Mars in 2013.
In 2020, India reformed its space policies to let private companies build and launch rockets, opening a new era of commercial space activity.

Skyroot Aerospace, founded in 2018 by former ISRO engineers, became the first private Indian company to reach space in 2022 with its suborbital Vikram-S rocket, paving the way for this orbital attempt.

The launch will take place at Satish Dhawan Space Centre (India's main spaceport on the Bay of Bengal), and the global small-satellite market is booming due to demand for internet, Earth observation, and navigation services.

perspectives.description: Space technology enthusiasts see this as a giant leap for India's private space sector, creating jobs and lowering launch costs globally. A successful launch could attract more investment and spark innovation.

Some critics point out that rocket launches contribute to space debris and carbon emissions. With more rockets, the risk of collisions in orbit increases, potentially making space more hazardous for future missions.

From a market perspective, the small-satellite launch industry is currently supply-constrained; few companies offer dedicated rides. Skyroot's entry could fill a gap, but it faces competition from established players like SpaceX's rideshare missions, which are already driving prices down.

If Vikram-1 succeeds, Skyroot envisions a future where Indian private rockets launch frequently, possibly from mobile sea-based pads, slashing costs and making space accessible to universities and small businesses.
